stories.body:
Jack Grealish is back in the Everton fold and could make his return in Monday's clash with Brentford.

The on-loan Manchester City midfielder has not featured for the Toffees for a month following a breach of club discipline but appeared in a behind-closed-doors match against Derby last week.

Everton boss David Moyes confirmed Grealish is fit and available, saying: "He's back in training and back in and around the team."

The 31-year-old issued a public apology on Instagram, to which Moyes said: "I don't do social media but I've heard about it."

On whether the pair have held talks, the Scot added: "We've just been getting on with our work.

- Predicting how all 20 Premier League teams will finish the season

- Jack Grealish issues public apology after making Everton comeback in friendly

"We've got a lot of other players who I need to put a lot of focus on as well, I can't just concentrate on one player. I've been trying to make sure that everybody's getting the right preparation and getting ready for our next game against Brentford."

At the start of his news conference Moyes was presented with a framed memento of his time in charge by defender James Tarkowski and former player Leon Osman after he set a new club record of 593 games in the hotseat.

Moyes said: "It's something that I'm really thrilled about but, if I'm being honest, it's not something I really think about. I understand I've suddenly become the manager who's had more games at Everton than anybody before and that's a real honour and privilege to be put in that position."

stories.headline: 2026-27 MLB free agency, trade grades: Offseason analysis
stories.summary: We've got you covered with grades and analysis on every winter signing and big offseason trade.
stories.body:
Hot stove season has finally begun!

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is officially here, and we have you covered with grades and analysis for every major signing and trade as this winter -- which is expected to include a labor stoppage -- unfolds.

Whether it's a franchise-changing free agent signing or an unexpected blockbuster trade, we'll weigh in with what it all means for next season and beyond.

ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle and David Schoenfield will evaluate each move as it happens, so follow along here, as this story will continue to be updated. Check back in for all the most recent analysis.

Related links: Tracker | Top 50 free agents

Yankees reinforce bullpen with Bednar, Loaisiga

The deals: David Bednar accepts one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer; Jonathan Loáisiga agrees to two-year, $18 million deal

Grade: C+

Let's combine these two moves into one overall grade as the Yankees piece together the back end of their bullpen -- a pen that ranked second in the majors with a 3.13 ERA in 2026. The Yankees shoved Bednar into a corner by giving him a qualifying offer, which promised to limit his demand in free agency since he would have been tied to draft pick compensation. By accepting it, Bednar's salary is now the highest average salary for a reliever, topping Edwin Diaz's $23 million with the Dodgers.

Other than a blip in 2024, Bednar has been steady since 2021, first with the Pirates and then with the Yankees after coming over at the trade deadline in 2025, posting sub-3.00 ERAs in five of his six seasons, including 2.47 ERA in 2026 when he racked up 35 saves in 39 opportunities. He throws a four-seamer, splitter and curveball, with his splitter his big out pitch, holding batters to a .149 average in 2026 and .175 in 2025, with just one home run over the two seasons. His four-seamer can be more hittable, although he kept it in the park this past season. The Yankees love his toughness and showed their high regard for him in giving him the qualifying offer. He's not an A-plus closer, but he's very good and a safe bet on a one-year -- albeit expensive -- deal.

Loáisiga, meanwhile, returns to the club where he pitched from 2018 to 2025 -- although "pitched" is a loose description since he was often injured. In his one year with Arizona, he posted a 2.42 ERA across 67 innings, just the second time he's surpassed 50 innings. He still has an electric 98 mph sinker, although he fanned just 48 batters. Even for a sinker-reliant pitcher, that's a low total, although he did produce a high ground ball rate and a lot of soft contact. We'll see how that works without Geraldo Perdomo and Nolan Arenado behind him.

The problem is the durability history, and Loáisiga is replacing free agent Paul Blackburn, who had an amazing year, with a 1.59 ERA in 85 innings. Loáisiga isn't going to match that ERA or throw that many innings -- but Blackburn was unlikely to do that again, either. Overall, the Yankees have at least locked in their closer and top right-handed setup guy, although they are paying a steep price at $32 million to do it. -- Schoenfield

Rockies add pair of starters in deal with White Sox

Colorado Rockies get:

RHP Davis Martin

RHP Luis Castillo

Chicago White Sox get:

LHP Sean Sullivan

C Douglas Veliz

White Sox grade: C+

The White Sox appear to be spending proverbial money to spend proverbial money. That is to say, they are moving past the Castillo mistake from the last trade deadline -- one whose ramifications were primarily monetary -- and to do it, they are folding in a legitimate starter in Martin -- a pitcher who, for the first few weeks of the 2026 season, looked like a Cy Young candidate. They aren't spending actual money but are rearranging resources in hopes of spending money in a more productive way.

That's just reality, not an attempt to overhype Martin, whose season came unraveled the deeper we got into the calendar and who was ultimately not in position to help Chicago's staff once it reached the postseason. Still, he put up more than 140 innings in each of the past two seasons with a 104 ERA+ during the pre-arbitration phase of his service time window. He was a valuable player for Chicago and therefore is now that for Colorado.

This perspective speaks to how badly the White Sox wanted to clear Castillo off their books, and his departure -- which rids them of a $22.75 million 2027 salary plus a semi-unlikely vesting option for 2028 -- opens up the payroll so that Chicago can further upgrade a rotation it thinks it upgraded with the signing of Dustin May earlier this week.

Castillo was ghastly -- harsh as that sounds -- last season for the Mariners before Chicago acquired him at the trade deadline, and he was even worse after the deal. It was the first truly bad season of his mostly very good 10-year big league career, but it felt like it was one that was a result of trends that were years in the making. The one and truly virtuous aspect of this deal for the White Sox is that it rids them of the considerable risk that Castillo bounces back and justifies his sizable salary.

Sullivan is a long, lean lefty with so-so stuff who relies on deception -- perhaps not the soft-tossing lefty of yore, but someone along those lines. Veliz is a 17-year-old catcher who originally was signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela. Maybe someday you'll read his name again.

Chicago's grade is entirely provisional. The White Sox have opened up payroll space that needs to be parlayed into a meaningful upgrade. The 2027 rotation, once it's in place, will have some kind of configuration that includes May, an unsigned pitcher to be named and the other returnees to the staff. The gamble is that this new group will be better than simply running it back with Castillo while hoping for more consistency from Martin.

Right now, it's hard to say which path would have been better.

Rockies grade: B

I mean, why not? It's easy to make the crude argument against Castillo -- over 126 games for the Mariners, he went 43-40 with a 3.69 ERA while pitching half the time in one of baseball's most pitcher-friendly contexts. (During those seasons, his ERA was 3.07 at T-Mobile Park and 4.38 on the road.) Now he's headed to the wood-chipper of a pitching context at Coors Field and doing so at the nadir of his career.

Still, for the Rockies, it's a worthy gamble especially since it lands them Martin in the process. Is Martin the right pitcher for Coors Field? Who knows? But the still-new brain trust in Colorado needs to show it has real ideas about who will and who will not be able to function from the pitcher's mound in the Rockies' home venue.

Martin has real remaining upside, but Castillo is really the intriguing part here because he's a veteran with a lot to prove given the lack of long-term certainty around his contract status. Maybe he's done. Fine. It's only money, right? And you've still got Martin. But if Castillo flourishes by whatever definition that means when pitching in Coors, it's more than a productive performance for a team likely to land once again in the NL West cellar. It's a proof of concept. The Rockies need all of those they can get. -- Doolittle

Twins bring Gray back to Minnesota
The deal: Two years, $55 million

Grade: B+

Sonny Gray had one of the best seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins back in 2023, when he made 32 starts, posted a 2.79 ERA and a 5.6 WAR, and finished second in the Cy Young Award voting. (He won just eight games, plagued by a lack of run support and a poor bullpen.) The Twins are hoping for a happy reunion, signing Gray to the largest total value free agent pitcher contract in franchise history (tied with a four-year deal for Ervin Santana back in 2015). The second year is a player option, so this could end up being a one-year deal.

This wasn't necessarily where everyone expected Gray to land, especially coming off a strong season with the Boston Red Sox. He finished 18-5, tied with Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead in wins, while posting a 2.72 ERA, good for eighth in the majors. While Gray had some injuries earlier in his career, he has been durable across the past four seasons, averaging 30 starts and 175 innings. That almost makes him Old Hoss Radbourn in today's game. While Gray's ERA has jumped all over the place, his FIP (fielding independent pitching) speaks to more consistency, with marks of 3.40, 2.83, 3.12, 3.39 and 3.47 going back to 2022.

The negatives: Gray is 37 years old and his strikeout rate took a big dip in 2026, dropping from 28.4% over the previous two seasons to 21.8%. That's still playable -- the MLB average for starting pitchers was 21.9% -- but it's something to watch. However, he's such a smart pitcher -- mixing in six different pitches with excellent command -- that he can succeed even with a lower K rate.

It's a nice move for the Twins, who ranked 22nd in rotation ERA this past season. They've indicated an intent to keep Joe Ryan. Plus, Pablo Lopez is aiming to be ready by Opening Day in his return from Tommy John surgery, so Minnesota could roll out a rotation of Gray, Ryan, Lopez, Taj Bradley (their top starter in 2026 with 4.4 WAR) and Bailey Ober, with Dean Kremer, Connor Prielipp and Zebby Matthews as depth. Ryan, Lopez, Ober and Kremer are all in the final years of their deals, so there are trade possibilities here, especially since Minnesota needs to improve the bullpen.

Gray's contract projection was for two years and $42 million, so the deal comes in higher than that; this might be par for the course for starting pitchers given Dustin May's inflated three-year, $52.5 million deal with the Chicago White Sox. In one sense, the best-case scenario for the Twins is if Gray has another good season and he opts out. If he does have a good season and Lopez bounces back, this has a chance to be a really nice rotation, with Prielipp having breakout potential in his second year. And a good rotation in the American League Central will make the Twins contenders. -- Schoenfield

Mariners add Garcia to infield in six-player swap

Seattle Mariners get:

IF Maikel Garcia

RHP James McArthur

RHP L.P. Langevin

Kansas City Royals get:

RHP Bryce Miller

RHP Logan Evans

LHP Jose Ferrer

Mariners grade: A-

Garcia is the best player in the deal, and the difference is enough to make this a slam dunk win for Seattle. Nagging injuries undermined Garcia's 2026 season after his breakout the year before; but even so, his contract and patience at the plate remained well above average, and he was still one of baseball's top defensive third basemen. While the injuries cost him in the power department and on the bases, Garcia is entering his age-27 season as a good bet to bounce back to All-Star form. His well-documented penchant for self-improvement also supports the argument for positive regression.

Under contract through 2031 on team-friendly terms, Garcia is a major upgrade at a soft spot on the Mariners' depth chart. Seattle's defensive projection at the hot corner leaped from 21st to first in my system, and the offensive leap in runs from that spot was about 10 spots, to No. 12. Garcia's range will only help the overall infield defense, as he will team with Colt Emerson, Cole Young and Josh Naylor to give Seattle a pretty dynamic group.

The Mariners had the kind of surplus on their organizational rotation chart to easily absorb the loss of Miller. Similar to last year, they look a little thin in bullpen lefties, but Ferrer didn't prove to be the splash addition in that role Seattle hoped for anyway. McArthur is a sneaky get here. He hasn't pitched in the majors since 2024 because of injury but was closing games for the Royals before getting hurt. He's a worthy flier. Langevin is a lower-level prospect, a righty with big strikeout rates and shaky command.

The Mariners' right-now win projection climbs over 90 with this trade, and at 67% division title odds, Seattle is a heavy early favorite in a soft division. This trade only bolsters the chances that the Mariners bounce back in 2027 to become the team we thought they were in 2026.

Royals grade: C-

The Royals just don't have the kind of organizational depth to be trading one of their few difference-makers for a package of pitchers who in total upgrade their staff only marginally and offer little collective upside. In the near term, the trade makes the Royals worse, and the problems only compound from here given that they had Garcia under team control for so long.

Miller moves right into a middle-of-the-rotation slot for the Royals, and if Michael Wacha declines, it's possible Miller will be Kansas City's top starter next season. Still, Miller, 27, has a career ERA+ of 95 and is at 80 over the past two seasons, both of which have been undermined by injury. For the Royals, the hope would be that Miller is ready to take the kind of leap that Wacha and Seth Lugo did when they joined the Royals. And to be fair, Miller's Statcast metrics definitely suggest that could happen.

Ferrer, as mentioned, had a poor season in Seattle after being acquired for catcher Harry Ford. Ferrer has a career OPS+ of 96 but still becomes the Royals' top bullpen lefty, almost by default. Evans was a ranked organizational prospect in Seattle and had a decent debut season in 2025. He underwent Tommy John surgery, the internal brace version, in January. He projected with mid- to lower-rotation upside before getting hurt.

The instant change in the Royals' projection kind of tells the story. The new pitchers are pushing not-great pitchers down the depth chart, so Kansas City's profile improves by about 16 runs on the prevention side. Garcia's defensive loss is fairly marginal for Kansas City, as Nick Loftin is a good defender, as well. But the loss of the bat is about a 17-run hit for the Royals' run production.

The end result? The same amount of bad, just shaped differently. The Royals should have received more for a player of Garcia's ability and contract. -- Doolittle

White Sox add midrotation piece with May
The deal: Three years, $52.5 million

Grade: D+

We've had two significant signings off the free agent market so far, and both involve freshly minted ex-Milwaukee Brewers: After Jake Bauers landed with the Boston Red Sox on Friday, the Chicago White Sox plucked Dustin May off the championship Milwaukee pitching staff.

Whereas Boston was banking on Bauers' 2026 breakout being his current true talent level, the White Sox are perhaps taking a bigger gamble that May's past five years do not represent his real level of ability. Since his early shine as a top Los Angeles Dodgers prospect, which included some promising early work in the majors, May's career has been journeyman-like. Around injuries that cost him the 2024 season, he has put up 0.9 bWAR with a 91 ERA+ over 356 big-league innings for the period covering 2022 through last season.

May became a fallback addition for the Brewers at the 2026 trade deadline after more glitzy pursuits (ahem, Tarik Skubal) fell short. May put up a 106 ERA+ for the St. Louis Cardinals before the trade and, given the Brewers' track record with acquired pitchers, you had to figure the move boded well for an even better post-trade performance. But that's not what happened. May had a 5.65 ERA and 75 ERA+ over 10 starts for the Brewers and was not a core part of Milwaukee's postseason rotation.

This uninspiring platform performance partially explains the grade above, but only partially. We'll see how things shake out in the market when we have more signings to work from -- May is the first pitcher to land a sizable deal -- but this seems like an overpay at least in terms of years. ESPN's Kiley McDaniel projected a one-year, $14 million deal for May, while a consensus projection from various outlets looked something more like two years, $24.7 million.

The White Sox are likely banking on May's tantalizing tracking data, which in 2026 had him in the 85th percentile in fastball velocity (average of 96.8 mph) and 72nd percentile in extension. Indeed, my own projection model sees enough in May keeping his value that it suggested a three-year, $45.9 million deal would be justified, which at least is in the neighborhood of what he got from the White Sox.

As it stands, May slots in behind Grant Taylor in the revamped Chicago rotation, just ahead of Sean Burke and Luis Castillo. Ah, Castillo: Is he a cautionary tale for a White Sox approach that liked him, as it likes May, despite underwhelming results before the deal? We'll see. May is also pushing pitchers such as David Sandlin and Davis Martin down in the pecking order, though there's no guarantee he's going to be that much better than them, if at all. I've got May adding 0.9 wins to Chicago's right-now roster, which pushes its 2027 playoff odds up by about three percentage points.

That's fairly marginal when you remember that the White Sox were overachievers in 2026. It was a great story, but it also means their starting baseline is somewhere south of the 84 games they won in 2026. If they are really looking to bolster their chances heading into 2027 -- and beyond -- then opportunity cost comes into play even though the White Sox should have some remaining spending capacity, or at least you would hope so. Would a little patience have netted them someone like Sonny Gray, Michael King or Freddy Peralta?

If the White Sox still go after someone like that and the May signing doesn't end up as their one big rotation splash, then maybe we push that grade up to the C-minus range. Given what we know at the moment, though, I'm underwhelmed. -- Doolittle

Red Sox get offensive boost with Bauers addition

The deal: Four years, $58 million

Grade: A

The Red Sox weren't high on anybody's list of teams likely to sign Jake Bauers given they already have an All-Star first baseman in Willson Contreras, but this signing is an early candidate for best move of the offseason. The grade reflects two thoughts: (1) that Bauers' breakout -- he finished 11th in the majors in OPS and third in on-base percentage this past season -- is for real; and (2) that the contract is a steal at $14.5 million per year.

Bauers will be entering his age-31 season, and, of course, spent years struggling in the majors before finally figuring things out, so while there would generally be concern that his 2026 season was a fluke, all the advanced metrics suggest the opposite. His Statcast numbers: 93rd percentile bat speed, 94th percentile hard-hit rate, 93rd percentile chase rate, 98th percentile walk rate. Those are real skills that aren't going to diminish overnight and should allow him to remain a productive hitter (he even hit left-handers well, so should project as a full-time player). Everyone saw the quality of his at-bats during the postseason throughout the Milwaukee Brewers' title run; he was named MVP of the National League Championship Series.

As for the contract, compare it to Josh Naylor's deal last year, when he signed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Seattle Mariners. Naylor was two years younger, but he was coming off a 129-OPS+, 3.0-WAR season compared with Bauers' 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR. Yes, Naylor had the longer track record of success but less power and a lower OBP. Signing Bauers for $58 million looks like a potential bargain.

Contreras is under contract for 2027 with a team option for 2028 and is the better fielder, so Bauers slots in as the DH. That leaves Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu in the outfield. Masataka Yoshida is still around for one more year as a backup, and the Red Sox will likely look to trade Jarren Duran, who still has two years of team control but is estimated to make $11.1 million in arbitration. With Duran coming off a bad season at the plate, the Red Sox might non-tender him if they can't trade him.

No doubt there will be criticism that the Red Sox needed a right-handed batter instead, but they actually had a slightly higher OPS against left-handers (.734 to .710). They just needed a good hitter, regardless of which side of the plate he stands on.

Remember that they also acquired the right-handed Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals only to see him get injured in his first game with them. He'll be back and should slot in at second base. Boston also has shortstop Franklin Arias, one of the top three or four prospects in the minors who demolished Double- and Triple-A this year. Indeed, if Bauers comes close to his 2026 numbers and Anthony hits like everyone thought he was going to in 2026, this could be one of the best lineups in the league:

LF Anthony (L)

RF Abreu (L)

1B Contreras (R)

DH Bauers (L)

CF Rafaela (R)

2B Mead (R)

C Adley Rutschman (S)

SS Arias (R) / Trevor Story (R)

3B Caleb Durbin (R)

As for the Brewers, it's sad to see a postseason hero go, although not necessarily unexpected. They could have afforded this contract, but they have first-base prospects just about ready in Andrew Fischer, who led the minors with 48 home runs, and Blake Burke, who hit 34 home runs and stole 29 bases. They also have Andrew Vaughn on hand as a placeholder if Fischer and Burke aren't ready. Plus, they might need this money to sign William Contreras to a long-term extension. The Brewers will be fine. -- Schoenfield

Braves bolster bullpen by landing Phillips
The deal: Three years, $35 million

Grade: B-

The Atlanta Braves don't go after the biggest free agents -- B.J. Upton's $75 million deal in 2013 remains the largest free agent contract in franchise history -- but president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos does like to strike as early as possible in the offseason, and he did that again with Evan Phillips.

Phillips will essentially take the roster spot of Raisel Iglesias, so the Braves will get a little younger and maybe a little better, although Iglesias had a good season as the closer in 2026 following some bumps in 2025. The Braves had one of the best bullpens in the majors this past year, leading in win probability added while ranking fourth in ERA and sixth in OPS allowed. Iglesias departs as a free agent, but Didier Fuentes or Robert Suarez can replace him as the ninth-inning guy, with Phillips likely slotting in as a setup man alongside lefties Dylan Lee and Dylan Dodd.

Phillips was one of the best relievers in the majors with the Dodgers in 2022-23 before suffering shoulder and elbow injuries at the end of the 2024 season and finally undergoing Tommy John surgery in June 2025. He returned to make 31 appearances with the Dodgers in 2026, finishing with 33 strikeouts and just six walks in 26 innings. The stuff looked good -- he was throwing a little harder than pre-injury -- although he did serve up five home runs, and his injury history makes a three-year deal a little risky.

The belief was that the Braves' pitching priority this offseason would be a starter, but signing Phillips will allow them to stretch out Fuentes as a starter in spring training. He does have a three-pitch arsenal in his fastball, slider and splitter, and he has thrown a curveball in the past, so as effective as Fuentes was in relief as a rookie in 2026, it makes sense to see if it can work out for him in the rotation. -- Schoenfield

Tigers kick off free agency with Pagan deal

The deal: One year, $11.5 million

Grade: C

A key reason the Detroit Tigers finished 76-86 despite a plus-71 run differential was the bullpen: Despite finishing 12th in ERA, it ranked 26th in win probability added, so it performed worse in high-leverage situations. Out with Kenley Jansen, in with Emilio Pagan, who has been the Reds' closer the past two seasons.

Jansen was only 22-for-28 in saves in 2026, so maybe Pagan is only a small upgrade, but like Jansen, Pagan has been prone to the home run, serving up 17 in 111⅓ innings over the past two seasons. The Tigers are betting that getting out of Cincinnati -- where he allowed 12 of those 17 home runs -- will help. Pagan is a three-pitch reliever, with a splitter that he throws primarily to left-handers and a cutter he throws to right-handers. But his 95 mph fastball is rather pedestrian for a modern closer, and batters have hit 12 home runs off it the past two seasons.

Pagan is also turning 36 years old and his fastball velo dropped from 95.8 mph in 2025 to 94.9 in 2026, so there are a couple of red flags here. The Tigers had to add somebody to the bullpen, and doing so before the anticipated lockout is logical, but Pagan projects as a midtier closer rather than the elite guy Detroit needs. Kyle Finnegan and Will Vest both struggled in 2026, so the Tigers could still nab a reliable right-handed setup guy. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: No relegation means MLS playing style more 'careless' - Whitecaps' Müller
stories.body:
Vancouver Whitecaps star Thomas Müller has said that because MLS does not have a promotion/relegation system, the players feel less pressure and the playing style is more "careless, defensively."

Müller, 37, who joined the Whitecaps in August 2025 and renewed his deal through next year, is the most decorated German player of all time. In his 17-year career with Bayern Munich, he won a record 13 Bundesliga titles, six DFB-Pokals, eight Supercups, two Champions Leagues, two UEFA Super Cups, and two FIFA Club World Cups.

When asked to compare MLS to the Premier League or other European Leagues, the 2014 World Cup winner said MLS playing style suffers without promotion and relegation.

"It's difficult to compare because of the system," he told Canadian media outlet Global News. "There is no relegation. There is no big pressure."

He said the lack of pressure means that players lack the attention "to be focused over 90 minutes."

"[In Europe with relegation] The players have maybe no contracts for next year when you go down, so the playing style changes," he said. "When you play a bottom of the league team in Europe they fight for their lives. And sometimes I have the feeling, because of the [MLS] system, the playing style is a little bit more, let's say, optimistic, or careless, defensively.

"So a little bit, just a little bit more, the French would say, laissez faire," he said. "That's maybe good for seeing some nice offensive plays when the games are opening up. When I compare it I see sometimes really, really good individual actions in players.

"What I miss sometimes is maybe the consistency, the good and the bad, the gap is bigger.

"But the good is, we can compare it with golf, you know, even a 10-handicapper has sometimes shots a professional couldn't do better. So it's maybe the free kick, top corner free kick. But the bad shots of a professional would be never that bad. And that's a little bit, sometimes it's more like the attention of the players to be focused over 90 minutes, that's what I see sometimes, they're lacking."

Müller, who helped the Whitecaps into the MLS Cup for the first time in the club's history in 2025, only to be beaten by Inter Miami CF and Lionel Messi, said the fear of relegation helps keep teams sharp.

"[In MLS] There is, oh yeah, we do a rebuild," he said. "Nobody is happy to lose but it's totally different when you fight for getting relegated. Maybe yeah, you lose budget for the next year, the whole club. You lose people working at the club when the budget changes. It's totally different for fans."

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: F1 bosses confirm 'agreement' on V8 engine return deal
stories.summary: McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.
stories.body:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.

Brown's comments follow a post on social media by FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem earlier this week that stated: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."

Ben Sulayem's post coincided with what appeared to be an official announcement on the FIA's own social media channels, only for those details to be quickly deleted.

Brown said on Thursday at the Las Vegas Grand Prix that there were still elements to be decided, but that the overarching agreement on V8 engines was in place.

"There's an agreement in principle," he said. "I think everyone is very, very excited. I think now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's."

The plan to introduce the new engine formula was discussed during a meeting of F1, the FIA, teams and power unit manufacturers on Tuesday in London.

Fast-tracking the change for 2030 would see the current engine regulation cycle, which was introduced at the start of this year, cut short by one year.

The existing regulations, which feature 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrids, have been criticised by drivers for being overcomplicated, with four-time champion Max Verstappen labelling the current power units "anti-racing" at the start of the year.

The plan discussed on Tuesday is for F1 to introduce 2.1-litre turbocharged V8s with a less powerful hybrid element than the current power units.

- Antonelli handed grid penalty for Las Vegas GP; Russell sets pace in FP2

- Max Verstappen on F1 retirement, Le Mans and learning to lose: 'Stress a bit less'

- FIA to introduce full-time stewards to address worries over decision-making

The next step is for the final proposal to be agreed upon and presented to the FIA's World Motor Sport Council in Shanghai next month.

Alpine team boss Flavio Briatore said the agreement for 2030 was all but signed.

"We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy," Briatore said. "I think it's the right way to go.

"We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that because, in the end, I believe the best for the spectator, for everybody is a very simple engine, a lot of noise and basta.

"Maybe have some KERS [Kinetic Energy Recovery Systems] or stuff like that, nothing major like we have now."

The current regulations, which require nearly 50% of peak power to come from the power unit's battery, were introduced to keep the sport road-car relevant and entice more engine manufacturers to F1.

In that sense they were successful, with Audi joining this season, Honda returning from the brink of leaving the sport to team up with Aston Martin, and Ford partnering with Red Bull's in-house powertrains department.

However, the emphasis on electric power has proved controversial this year, with drivers forced to change their driving style to manage energy around a lap instead of pushing the cars to the limit.

Two-time champion Fernando Alonso labelled this year's regulations a "battery world championship" following the second race of the season in China, with the sport later agreeing to tweak certain rules to limit the unusual behaviour of the hybrid systems by the fourth round in Miami.

Further changes are planned over the next two seasons to shift the 50/50 split between electrical power and internal combustion engine (ICE) power to 60/40 in favour of the ICE by 2028.

V8 engines were last used in F1 in 2013 and featured a mild hybrid boost known as the Kinetic Energy Recovery System.

The previous era of V8s were known for their evocative exhaust note, but the turbocharged versions proposed for 2030 are not expected to be as loud or high-pitched due to the presence of a turbocharger.

stories.headline: 2027 WNBA mock draft: Tempo win lottery, projected to pick JuJu Watkins at No. 1
stories.summary: Toronto edged Houston and got the top pick in Sunday's draft lottery. The Comets will pick No. 2 and the Mystics No. 3.
stories.body:
In what could be the JuJu Watkins sweepstakes, the Toronto Tempo will have the No. 1 pick in the 2027 WNBA draft. The Tempo won the draft lottery Sunday, with the Houston Comets picking second and the Washington Mystics third.

The Seattle Storm have the No. 4 pick, the Portland Fire got No. 5 and the Los Angeles Sparks have Nos. 6 and 7.

The Tempo, an expansion team in 2026, finished 11-33 last season, missing the playoffs. They were last in the league in defensive rating and won just one game after the All-Star break.

All of that could be much improved in 2027 with a player such as Watkins in Toronto. The national player of the year as a sophomore for the USC Trojans, Watkins missed last season after a knee injury suffered in the 2025 NCAA tournament. She has looked great so far this season and would fit in well with any WNBA team.

This is just Watkins' third college season, but age-wise, she is eligible for the draft. It is unknown if she will go pro or return to USC, but for now we are including her in the mock draft. If she decides Toronto is an unappealing destination or just wants to spend another season in college, she can wait until the 2028 draft.

That said, there is also uncertainty about the seniors who already have completed three seasons. Under the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model -- the five-seasons-in-five-years rule -- they could return for the 2027-28 season. So a lot about the draft pool remains speculative.

But now we know the lottery order.

1. Toronto Tempo: JuJu Watkins
USC | guard | 6-foot-2 | senior

Watkins and the Trojans are 3-1 after a close loss Sunday to No. 1 South Carolina in which she had 25 points. The March 2025 knee injury that forced Watkins to miss last season has not slowed her. She is averaging 24.5 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 3.3 steals. The Tempo's strength last season was at guard, led by Marina Mabrey. If Watkins doesn't declare for the draft, there should still be good players available for the Tempo. But perhaps not an immediate franchise-changer as Watkins is expected to be.

2. Houston Comets: Madison Booker
Texas | forward | 6-foot-1 | senior

Like several teams, Texas has not been tested yet. But Booker has displayed why she's a lottery pick in the three games she has played so far, including a 30-point, six-assist game against Northern Colorado. Booker's size, strength and confidence on offense and her versatility on defense should translate to the pro game. She took a hard fall in Wednesday's win over South Dakota State and did not play in Sunday's victory against Tarleton State, but she is not expected to miss much more time. The Comets -- the Connecticut Sun relocated as a revived franchise -- last played in the 2008 WNBA season. The Sun were tied for next to last with Toronto at 11-33 this year, and it's fair to say they could use help in all areas, which would make Booker appealing.

3. Washington Mystics: Hannah Hidalgo
Notre Dame | guard | 5-foot-6 | senior

Hidalgo has carried a heavy load throughout her college career, and that continues her senior season. In four victories, she has averaged 28.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 4.8 steals while shooting 59.4% from the field. Hidalgo is a huge threat on offense and defense and could really add to the young core already there if she goes to the Mystics. Washington could use more 3-point shooting. While Hidalgo wasn't great from beyond the arc last season (36 of 142, 25.4%), she shot 40% from 3-point range as a sophomore and is at 40% so far this season.

4. Seattle Storm: Tessa Johnson
South Carolina | guard | 6-foot-1 | senior

Johnson's 3-point shooting is an impressive tool that will translate to the pro game. She was the top power-conference player in the country last season in 3-point percentage (44.8%, 90 of 201). So far this season, she is 9-for-18 (50%) from beyond the arc and is averaging 17.0 points. She had 28 points in Sunday's victory over USC. The Storm were last in the WNBA this past season at 8-36 and could benefit from another dynamic young guard to go along with the young post talent they have.

5. Portland Fire: Mikaylah Williams
LSU | guard | 6-foot | senior

The Tigers have cruised through four blowouts, and Williams' averages -- 19.0 points, 5.3 rebounds and 5.5 assists while shooting 58% from the field and 45.5% from beyond the arc -- don't tell us anything we didn't expect. She's a pro-ready player on the offensive end who can look to improve defensively in the WNBA. The expansion Fire had a solid season in 2025, going 17-27, and Williams could fit in offensively.

6. Los Angeles Sparks: Kymora Johnson
Virginia | guard | 5-foot-7 | senior

The Cavaliers are 5-0, and we will know more about them once they play their tougher nonconference foes, such as Oklahoma on Nov. 23. But so far, Johnson has looked very good, averaging 18.8 points, 5.2 rebounds, 5.4 assists and 2.2 steals while shooting 59.6% from the field and 61.3% from beyond the arc (13 of 21). With back-to-back picks, Los Angeles can address two of several needs with this draft. The Sparks were 16-28 this season and missed the playoffs for the sixth year in a row.

7. Los Angeles Sparks: Sarah Cissé
France | forward | 6-foot-2

There's so much we don't know now about the Sparks -- including who their coach will be for 2027 -- as they move on after future Hall of Famer Nneka Ogwumike's retirement. But Cissé is another talented player out of France who could make an impact on the WNBA. The MVP of the U20 European Championships this summer, she turns 20 in January. The Sparks were next to last in the WNBA in rebounding this past season, so Cissé might be able to help there.

8. New York Liberty: Ainhoa Risacher
France | forward | 6-foot-1

If you recognize the last name, Risacher is the younger sister of Zaccharie Risacher, the NBA's No. 1 draft pick in 2024. A good-sized wing player, Risacher competed alongside Cissé on France's winning U20 European Championships team this past summer. She will turn 20 in July. The Liberty had an up-and-down 2026 season, getting the No. 8 seed in the playoffs. They knocked off No. 1 Minnesota but then were swept by No. 4 Atlanta. New York fired Chris DeMarco after just one season, so we await their next coach. The Liberty already have a strong French/international presence. The question might be if Risacher impresses them enough defensively compared with other draft options.

9. Dallas Wings: Chloe Kitts
South Carolina | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Kitts missed last season because of a knee injury but has looked great so far. A starter as a junior, she averaged 10.2 points and 7.7 rebounds in 2024-25. Through four games this season, she has three double-doubles and is averaging 13.0 points and 10.0 rebounds. In Sunday's victory over USC, Kitts had 15 points, 12 rebounds, three assists and four steals. If she continues to play this well, we could see her move up the draft board. Still, with Dallas having young guards such as Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, Kitts could be a good addition for the Wings, who made the playoffs at 27-17 this season.

10. Indiana Fever: Talaysia Cooper
Ole Miss | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

The Fever are facing two huge offseason questions: Will free agent guard Kelsey Mitchell return, and who will be their general manager? Indiana could use help at the wing position with a player who can defend at a high level but also score. That could be Cooper, who is playing for her third SEC program and averaging 14.0 points while shooting 37% (10 of 27) from 3-point range. She showed progress from beyond the arc last season, and if that continues this season it will help her draft prospects. Cooper had her best defensive season as a sophomore at Tennessee, and a return to that level will boost her.

11. Chicago Sky: Khamil Pierre
NC State | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Pierre doesn't shoot the 3 much, but she is relentless in the paint. After two strong years at Vanderbilt, she transferred to NC State and led the ACC in rebounding last season (11.9 RPG) while averaging 16.7 points and shooting 52.5% from the field. So far this season for the 4-1 Wolfpack, she is averaging 21.2 points and 8.4 rebounds while shooting 51.3%. The injury-plagued Sky went 16-28 and missed the playoffs for the third year in a row this past season. They were 13th in offensive rating and 10th in rebounding, and Pierre might help in both areas.

12. Chicago Sky: S'Mya Nichols
Kansas | guard | 6-foot | senior

Nichols is off to a little slower start than expected, averaging 12.5 points and 4.3 assists. (She averaged 17.4 and 4.6 last season.) That's why she has fallen from No. 6 in our two previous mock drafts. But to be fair, it's still early in the season. Nichols had 12 points and six assists in the Jayhawks' loss to Nebraska on Saturday. She and Kansas have another shot at a ranked team this week at Minnesota on Wednesday.

13. Dallas Wings: Kaylene Smikle
Tennessee | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

Smikle started her career at Rutgers, then went to Maryland and is now at Tennessee. She played just seven games last year with the Terps, missing the rest of the season after knee surgery. So far this season, she is leading the 4-0 Lady Vols with 22.3 points per game, while also averaging 6.0 rebounds. She is also off to a hot start from beyond the arc at 50% (12 of 24). Smikle could add guard/wing depth for Dallas.

14. Golden State Valkyries: Oluchi Okananwa
Maryland | guard | 5-foot-10 | senior

Okananwa is averaging 14.0 points and 6.3 rebounds, but the Terps have played just three games. She was first-team All-Big Ten and all-defense last season -- we know the WNBA champion Valkyries love defense -- but she probably will need to show improvement as a 3-point shooter to ensure being a first-round pick. So far this season she is 3-for-6 from beyond the arc.

15. Minnesota Lynx: Clara Strack
Kentucky | center | 6-foot-5 | senior

Sunday was another big stats day for Strack, who had 29 points and 18 rebounds in a victory over Eastern Michigan. That included going 4-of-5 from beyond the arc, which is important: It's not easy for traditional centers to find their way in the WNBA, so having shooting range matters. Strack has shown that, making 42 3-pointers over the past two seasons. She is 8-of-21 from 3-point range so far this season. Strack, who was the SEC's defensive player of the year in 2025, is averaging 18.4 points, 9.6 rebounds and 3.8 blocks for the 5-0 Wildcats.

stories.headline: Abu Dhabi court reduces sentences for 8 in Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili brawl
stories.summary: An Abu Dhabi court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, for their part in last week's wild hotel brawl in the UAE's capital city.
stories.body:
Abu Dhabi's Criminal Court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants convicted in connection to last week's hotel brawl involving Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili, according to the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department.

The eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, were originally sentenced to six months in prison. Under the revised ruling, which the ADJD released Tuesday, each defendant will instead pay a fine of 150,000 AED (approximately $40,800). The department said the reduced sentence followed a reconciliation between the parties, the mutual withdrawal of claims and appeal by the victim to the Abu Dhabi government for their release.

The altercation took place Nov. 11 in the lobby of the Yas Hilton Hotel, ahead of RAF's inaugural event in Abu Dhabi. Multiple videos captured Nurmagomedov, who is the PFL lightweight champion and younger cousin of Khabib Nurmagomedov, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face, triggering a brawl between multiple members of both teams. Dvalishvili, who was initially arrested but released, advocated for Nurmagomedov's release Saturday.

Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili have been involved in a long-running feud, dating back to Dvalishvili's UFC title win against Umar Nurmagomedov, Usman's older brother, in January 2025. The camps were involved in a brief altercation at another RAF event in July in Dvalishvili's home country of Georgia. Over the weekend, UFC president Dana White criticized RAF's security measures, saying, "They must like it for this to happen all the time."

RAF founder Chad Bronstein told ESPN the organization regretted the incident, but pushed back on any suggestion it's becoming commonplace.

"Did they have drama in the past? Yeah," Bronstein said of Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili. "But did I think that was going to happen in Abu Dhabi? No. You can always expect there's going to be some words in a press conference ... I didn't think that would happen in a hotel lobby. How many fights have taken place at the UFC, at press conferences, in arenas? We have a great relationship with the UFC, but I think that's an unfair statement."

Bronstein added the incident did not impact RAF's recently-signed deal with the region of Abu Dhabi.

"We're already talking about new events coming up, we have a five-year deal," Bronstein said. "Saturday's event sold out Etihad Arena. I feel like there's going to be a long partnership."

On Monday, RAF announced Dvalishvili and his 21-year-old Georgian teammate Saba Lazishvili have been booked to the promotion's first event in the New York metropolitan area on Dec. 19 at Nassau Coliseum in Long Island.

Dvalishvili will face Kenzo Biyong, a former Dutch professional soccer player from the Netherlands. Lazashvili, who gained a massive online following for his participation in the hotel lobby brawl, will face the winner of a match between Sergio Garcia and Cody Garbrandt at RAF 15 on Nov. 28 in Chicago.

stories.headline: First-half romp powers Jillaroos' fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup salute
stories.summary: Australia's Jillaroos have blown away New Zealand 34-10 to win a fourth-straight Women's Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Australia have underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 annihilation of New Zealand in the World Cup final.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Suncorp Stadium, with winger Jaime Chapman recording a brilliant hat-trick before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

Her treble gave her the equal record for tries in a World Cup -- for men or women -- at 13, matching the Kiwi Ferns' Honey Hireme-Smiler from 2017.

It seemed inevitable that she would go clear in the second half.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Kiwi Ferns' try in the finals seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

For the Jillaroos there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Prop Millie Elliott retires with a fairytale ending while dual international Sariah Paki, who was chased by the Ferns to play for them, has now won the World Cup in two sports after triumphing with the Australian rugby sevens side in 2022.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.
